claim: Erectile dysfunction affects 5-35% of men aged 40-70 in varying degrees.
source: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is an age-dependent vascular disease, affecting 5–35% of men aged 40–70 in varying degrees (Kubin et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kubin et al., 2003.

claim: 322 million men worldwide will be affected by erectile dysfunction by 2025.
source: Although not fatal, 322 million men worldwide will be affected by the disease by 2025 (Ayta et al., 1999; Kessler et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ayta et al., 1999 and Kessler et al., 2019.

claim: Erectile dysfunction occurs in up to 75% of diabetes cases.
source: Moreover, it occurs in up to 75% of diabetes cases (Sáenz de Tejada et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sáenz de Tejada et al., 2002.

claim: Erectile dysfunction causes significant physical and psychological problems for patients and their families.
source: This causes significant physical and psychological problems for patients and their families (Bivalacqua et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bivalacqua et al., 2003.

claim: Cavernous tissue malfunction is considered a biomarker in the progression of cardiovascular and vascular diseases.
source: Moreover, the cavernous tissue is more prone to this disease than other blood vessels; therefore, its malfunction is considered as a biomarker in the progression of cardiovascular and vascular diseases (Miner, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Miner, 2011.

claim: Patients with severe vascular disease, such as diabetic ED, are less responsive to PDE5 inhibitors.
source: Current ED treatment involves the use of phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitors, but patients with severe vascular disease, such as diabetic ED, are less responsive.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Severe vascular dysfunction caused by diabetes results in insufficient bioavailable nitric oxide for PDE5 inhibitors to induce penile erection.
source: This is mainly because severe vascular dysfunction caused by diabetes results in insufficient bioavailable nitric oxide (NO) for PDE5 inhibitors to induce penile erection (Angulo et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Angulo et al., 2010.

claim: Pericytes interact with endothelial cells and are essential for penile erection.
source: Pericytes are vital in the pathogenesis of erectile function as their interactions with endothelial cells are essential for penile erection.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Pericytes are involved in angiogenesis, vasoconstriction, and permeability.
source: Pericytes interact with various cell types (especially endothelial cells) and are involved in angiogenesis, vasoconstriction, and permeability (Bergers and Song, 2005; Gerhardt and Betsholtz, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bergers and Song, 2005 and Gerhardt and Betsholtz, 2003.

claim: Diabetes causes pericyte loss or dysfunction, leading to vascular diseases.
source: Diabetes causes pericyte loss or dysfunction, thereby creating an imbalance between pericytes and endothelial cells, leading to vascular diseases (Liu et al., 2021; Warmke et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021 and Warmke et al., 2016.

claim: Diabetic retinopathy is characterized by pericyte loss, capillary basement membrane thickening, and increased permeability.
source: For example, diabetic retinopathy is characterized by pericyte loss, capillary basement membrane thickening, and increased permeability, leading to retinal hypoxia and inflammation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Pericytes are particularly sensitive to glucose oxidation, which promotes pericyte apoptosis.
source: Pericytes are particularly sensitive to glucose oxidation, which further promotes pericyte apoptosis (Warmke et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warmke et al., 2016.

claim: Advanced glycation end products accumulate in pericytes under hyperglycemic conditions.
source: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) accumulate in pericytes under hyperglycemic conditions, thereby stimulating the secretion of transforming growth factor beta in peripheral nerve pericytes, leading to basement membrane thickening, neovascularization, and pericyte apoptosis (Shimizu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shimizu et al., 2011.

claim: Restoring the content and function of cavernous pericytes significantly reduced the permeability of cavernous blood vessels and enhanced neurovascular regeneration.
source: Furthermore, our previous studies showed that restoring the content and function of cavernous pericytes significantly reduced the permeability of cavernous blood vessels and enhanced neurovascular regeneration (Yin et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yin et al., 2015, 2020, and 2021.

claim: Diabetes mellitus leads to smooth muscle cell dysfunction, such as decreased cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation.
source: Diabetes mellitus (DM) leads to SMC dysfunction, such as decreased cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation, resulting in an inability to obtain or maintain satisfactory erection (Reddy et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2016 and Wei et al., 2012.

claim: Marker genes of pericytes and smooth muscle cells often overlap, and their expression patterns are tissue-specific.
source: Since the marker genes of pericytes and SMCs often overlap, and their expression patterns are tissue-specific, identifying suitable in vivo markers to accurately interpret transcriptional and phenotypic changes in these cell types is of utmost importance (Chasseigneaux et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017; Smyth et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chasseigneaux et al., 2018, Kumar et al., 2017, and Smyth et al., 2018.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing has identified pericyte-specific markers in different tissues.
source: Recent studies have identified pericyte-specific markers in different tissues using single-cell RNA sequencing (Baek et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022), enabling characterization of various cell types and their cell-cell communication.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baek et al., 2022 and Sun et al., 2022.

claim: 12,894 cells were profiled in the single-cell transcriptome analysis of mouse cavernous tissue.
source: To elucidate the cellular landscape of mouse cavernous tissue and transcriptional changes in diabetic ED at the cellular level, we conducted a single-cell transcriptome analysis, profiling 12,894 cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The cells were grouped into 15 clusters based on their transcriptomic patterns.
source: The cells were grouped into 15 clusters based on their transcriptomic patterns, and cell types were annotated based on the expression of marker genes (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B and C.

claim: Clustering analysis identified fibroblasts, chondrocytes, myofibroblasts, lymphatic endothelial cells, valve-related LEC, vascular endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, and macrophages.
source: Clustering analysis identified fibroblasts (FBs), chondrocytes (Chonds), myofibroblasts (MFBs), lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC), valve-related LEC, vascular endothelial cells (VEC), SMCs, pericytes, Schwann cells, and macrophages.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Nos3 decreased in diabetic valve-related LEC and VEC.
source: We found that Nos3 (highly expressed in the untreated diabetes group compared to the treatment group) decreased in diabetic valve-related LEC and VEC (Ismail et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data and a citation to Ismail et al., 2020.

claim: Igfbp2 and Igfbp4 were downregulated in diabetic smooth muscle cells and chondrocytes, respectively.
source: In addition, Igfbp2 and Igfbp4 (lowly expressed in the penis of diabetic rats) were also downregulated in diabetic SMCs and Chonds, respectively, whereas Igfbp3 was upregulated in diabetic FB and MFB (Abdelbaky et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by data and a citation to Abdelbaky et al., 1998.

claim: Collagen genes were significantly underexpressed in diabetic fibroblasts, chondrocytes, myofibroblasts, and pericytes compared to normal tissues.
source: Collagen genes (vital in the corpus cavernosum structure) were significantly underexpressed in diabetic FB, Chond, My-FB, and pericytes than in normal tissues (Sullivan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by data and a citation to Sullivan et al., 2005.

claim: Genes associated with collagen or extracellular matrix organization and angiogenesis were downregulated in diabetic fibroblasts, chondrocytes, myofibroblasts, valve-related LEC, and pericytes compared to normal conditions.
source: Gene ontology analysis using differentially expressed genes (DEGs) indicated that the genes associated with collagen or extracellular matrix organization and angiogenesis were downregulated in diabetic FB, Chonds, MFBs, valve-related LEC, and pericytes compared to the cells under normal conditions (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Diabetic mice showed an increase in ribosome- and translation-related terms.
source: In contrast, diabetic mice showed an increase in ribosome- and translation-related terms (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no significant differentially expressed genes between diabetic and normal Schwann cells.
source: In Schwann cells, there were no significant DEGs between diabetic and normal cells.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Known marker genes for smooth muscle cells and pericytes were co-expressed in each cell type rather than being exclusively expressed.
source: However, rather than being exclusively expressed in each cell type, known marker genes were co-expressed in each cell type.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Gene sets related to the regulation of blood vessels and leukocytes were enriched in pericytes.
source: Gene sets related to the regulation of blood vessels and leukocytes were enriched in pericytes, whereas gene sets related to actin or muscles were enriched in SMC, suggesting that these clusters were properly annotated.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: Gene sets related to actin or muscles were enriched in smooth muscle cells.
source: Gene sets related to the regulation of blood vessels and leukocytes were enriched in pericytes, whereas gene sets related to actin or muscles were enriched in SMC, suggesting that these clusters were properly annotated.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: Six genes (Lbh, Ednra, Gpc3, Npy1r, Pln, and Atp1b2) were highly expressed in the pericyte cluster.
source: In addition, we screened six genes (Lbh, Ednra, Gpc3, Npy1r, Pln, and Atp1b2) that were highly expressed in the pericyte cluster from the single-cell analysis results (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rgs5 had the highest AUC score among pericyte markers.
source: When we calculate area under the curve (AUC) scores for the markers, Rgs5 had the highest AUC, but Rgs5 was also expressed in SMCs in our data (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by AUC score calculation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lbh was more specific for pericytes than Rgs5 in the single-cell data.
source: In the single-cell data, Lbh (Limb Bud-Heart) was more specific for pericytes than Rgs5, a well-known marker for distinguishing between SMC and pericytes (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: LBH was optimally expressed in mouse cavernous pericytes, whereas it was rarely expressed in the smooth muscle cells of the aorta.
source: IF staining showed that LBH was optimally expressed in MCP, whereas it was rarely expressed in the SMC of the aorta, consistent with our single-cell data (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the bladder blood vessels, α-SMA-expressing smooth muscle cells or CD31-expressing endothelial cells were surrounded by Lbh-expressing pericytes but rarely overlap.
source: In the blood vessels of other organ such as the bladder, α-SMA-expressing SMC or CD31-expressing endothelial cells were surrounded by Lbh-expressing pericytes but rarely overlap (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2E.

claim: LBH expression is more specific than PDGFRβ in mouse dorsal vein and dorsal artery tissues in penile tissue.
source: LBH expression was easily distinguishable from CD31 or α-SMA in mouse dorsal vein and dorsal artery tissues in penile tissue (Figure 2F, top panel), and is more specific than traditional pericyte markers (PDGFRβ) (Figure 2G, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: PDGFRβ is expressed in pericytes and other surrounding tissue cells.
source: For instance, PDGFRβ is expressed in pericytes and other surrounding tissue cells (as indicated by arrows and dotted area).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Angiogenesis-related interactions, including VEGF and fibroblast growth factor, were reduced between pericytes and other cell types in diabetes compared to normal conditions.
source: In diabetes, angiogenesis-related interactions, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor, were reduced between pericytes and other cell types compared to those under normal conditions (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Interactions related to neuronal survival, adhesion, migration, and proliferation decreased in diabetic mice.
source: In addition, interactions related to neuronal survival, adhesion, migration, and proliferation decreased in diabetic mice, as opposed to an increase in BMP signaling-related interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: The overall gene sets associated with angiogenesis, adhesion, and cell migration in pericytes were downregulated under diabetic conditions.
source: In addition to cell-cell interactions, the overall gene sets associated with angiogenesis, adhesion, and cell migration in pericytes were downregulated under diabetic conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Transcription factors promoting angiogenesis (Klf5, Egr1, Lmo2, Junb, and Elk1) were significantly more active in normal pericytes than in diabetic pericytes.
source: In normal pericytes, TFs promoting angiogenesis (Klf5, Egr1, Lmo2, Junb, and Elk1) were significantly more active than in diabetic pericytes (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Transcription factors that inhibit angiogenesis (Ppard and Hoxd10) were more active in diabetes.
source: In contrast, TFs that inhibit angiogenesis (Ppard and Hoxd10) were more active in diabetes.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network analysis.

claim: The expression of OPN, CD105, TSP-2, IGFBP2, and IGFBP9 decreased under diabetic conditions in cavernous tissue.
source: Furthermore, using the proteome profiler mouse angiogenesis array, we tested 53 angiogenesis factors in cavernous tissue, among which the expression of OPN (Dai et al., 2009), CD105 (Browne et al., 2018), TSP-2 (Kyriakides et al., 2001), IGFBP2 (Li et al., 2020), and IGFBP9 (Lin et al., 2003) decreased under diabetic conditions, while MMP-3 (Abdul et al., 2023), angiogenin (Neubauer-Geryk et al., 2012), and PF4 (Cella et al., 1986) increased (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteome profiler array data shown in Figure 3F and citations.

claim: MMP-3, angiogenin, and PF4 increased under diabetic conditions in cavernous tissue.
source: Furthermore, using the proteome profiler mouse angiogenesis array, we tested 53 angiogenesis factors in cavernous tissue, among which the expression of OPN (Dai et al., 2009), CD105 (Browne et al., 2018), TSP-2 (Kyriakides et al., 2001), IGFBP2 (Li et al., 2020), and IGFBP9 (Lin et al., 2003) decreased under diabetic conditions, while MMP-3 (Abdul et al., 2023), angiogenin (Neubauer-Geryk et al., 2012), and PF4 (Cella et al., 1986) increased (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteome profiler array data shown in Figure 3F and citations.

claim: LBH and CD140b expression significantly decreased in pericytes under diabetic conditions compared to age-matched controls.
source: We found that LBH and CD140b expression significantly decreased in the pericytes under diabetic conditions compared to those in age-matched controls (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: LBH expression was significantly decreased in mouse cavernous pericytes under diabetic conditions compared to normal conditions in vitro.
source: In addition, we assessed the expression of LBH in vitro under diabetic conditions and found that its expression was significantly decreased compared to that under normal conditions in MCPs (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: LBH overexpression in diabetic mice significantly improved the ratios of maximal and total intracavernous pressure to mean systolic blood pressure, reaching 84% of the control values.
source: However, LBH overexpression in diabetic mice significantly improved this erection parameter, reaching 84% of the control values (Figure 4G and H and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by erectile function measurement data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: LBH overexpression significantly improved the endothelial cell, pericyte, and neuronal cell contents in diabetic mice.
source: Moreover, IF staining for CD31 (an endothelial cell marker), NG2 (a pericyte marker), neurofilament-2000 (NF), and neuronal NOS (nNOS) revealed that LBH overexpression significantly improved the endothelial cell, pericyte, and neuronal cell contents in diabetic mice (Figure 4I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4I–N.

claim: LBH overexpression induced decreased apoptosis, increased proliferation, migration, and tube formation in cavernosum tissues under diabetic conditions.
source: These effects were achieved by inducing the survival cells in the cavernosum tissues (such as decreased apoptosis, increased proliferation, migration, and tube formation) and major pelvic ganglion (MPG) neurite sprouting under diabetic conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: LBH overexpression induced major pelvic ganglion neurite sprouting under diabetic conditions.
source: These effects were achieved by inducing the survival cells in the cavernosum tissues (such as decreased apoptosis, increased proliferation, migration, and tube formation) and major pelvic ganglion (MPG) neurite sprouting under diabetic conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: LBH is highly expressed in human cavernous pericytes.
source: Using a previous single-cell transcriptomics data of the human corpus cavernosum (Zhao et al., 2022), we examined whether LBH is highly expressed in human cavernous pericytes and has a similar role in diabetic conditions (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Further clustering of a smooth muscle cell cluster identified three subclusters: myofibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and pericytes.
source: Further clustering of an SMC cluster (marker: ACTA2) in the previous study identified three subclusters: ACTA2-expressing cluster as myofibroblasts (MFBs), CNN1-expressing cluster as SMCs, and RGS5- and LBH-expressing clusters as pericytes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Gene ontology analysis identified terms related to pericyte function (angiogenesis and leukocyte migration) in LBH-expressing pericytes.
source: Gene ontology analysis using DEGs between these clusters identified terms related to pericyte function in LBH-expressing pericytes (angiogenesis and leukocyte migration) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LBH expression was significantly reduced in human cavernous tissues from patients with diabetes-induced erectile dysfunction compared to age-matched controls.
source: The newly identified pericyte marker, LBH is also a marker of pericytes in the human corpus cavernosum, and LBH expression was significantly reduced in human cavernous tissues from patients with diabetes-induced ED compared to age-matched controls (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 5D and F.

claim: LBH expression was significantly reduced in primary cultured human cavernous pericytes under diabetic conditions compared to normal glucose conditions.
source: Furthermore, LBH expression was significantly reduced in primary cultured human cavernous pericytes under diabetic conditions compared to normal glucose (NG) conditions (Figure 5E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 5E and G.

claim: αB-crystallin (CRYAB) and Vimentin (VIM) were identified as LBH-interacting proteins in mouse cavernous pericytes through LC-MS/MS analysis.
source: We identified αB-crystallin (CRYAB) from band 1 and Vimentin (VIM) from bands 2 and 3, co-immunoprecipitated with LBH, VIM, and CRYAB (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: LBH co-localized with CRYAB and VIM in mouse cavernous tissues and mouse cavernous pericytes.
source: Furthermore, double IF staining indicated that LBH co-localized with CRYAB and VIM in mouse cavernous tissues and MCPs (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Proteins in the LBH-CRYAB-VIM network are mainly involved in neurogenesis, neuronal development, and the nervous system.
source: To identify the molecular mechanisms underlying interactions of LBH, CRYAB, and VIM, we performed gene ontology analysis using proteins from the PPI network. We found that these proteins are mainly involved in neurogenesis, neuronal development, and the nervous system (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Gene sets related to angiogenesis and the nervous system were enriched in normal pericytes compared to diabetic pericytes.
source: GSEA showed that gene sets related to angiogenesis and the nervous system were enriched in normal pericytes compared to diabetic pericytes (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CRYAB expression significantly reduced in vitro and in vivo under diabetic conditions.
source: Finally, we found that CRYAB expression significantly reduced in vitro and in vivo under diabetic conditions, whereas VIM expression significantly increased (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: VIM expression significantly increased in vitro and in vivo under diabetic conditions.
source: Finally, we found that CRYAB expression significantly reduced in vitro and in vivo under diabetic conditions, whereas VIM expression significantly increased (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: CRYAB promotes angiogenesis.
source: Previous studies have shown that CRYAB promotes angiogenesis (Dimberg et al., 2008) and interacts with LBH in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells, where it enhances cell survival by inhibiting the autoproteolytic maturation of caspase-3 (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dimberg et al., 2008.

claim: CRYAB interacts with LBH in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells and enhances cell survival by inhibiting the autoproteolytic maturation of caspase-3.
source: Previous studies have shown that CRYAB promotes angiogenesis (Dimberg et al., 2008) and interacts with LBH in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells, where it enhances cell survival by inhibiting the autoproteolytic maturation of caspase-3 (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: VIM is a type III intermediate filament protein expressed in mesenchymal cells.
source: VIM is a type III intermediate filament protein expressed in mesenchymal cells (Dave and Bayless, 2014; Guo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dave and Bayless, 2014 and Guo et al., 2013.

claim: VIM is involved in cell adhesion, migration, cellular integrity, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and the malignant transformation and metastatic spread of cancer cells.
source: It is involved in cell adhesion, migration, cellular integrity, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and the malignant transformation and metastatic spread of cancer cells (Chen et al., 2021; Dave and Bayless, 2014; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021, Dave and Bayless, 2014, and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: VIM interacts with the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor and promotes axonal extension.
source: For example, VIM interacts with the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor, promotes axonal extension, and serves as a double-edged sword in the nervous system by regulating axonal regeneration, myelination, apoptosis, and neuroinflammation (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2023.

claim: VIM knockout mice were less susceptible to bacterial infections and had a reduced inflammatory response compared to wild-type mice.
source: Furthermore, VIM knockout mice were less susceptible to bacterial infections and had a reduced inflammatory response than wild-type mice (Moisan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moisan et al., 2007.

claim: VIM deficiency prevents obesity and insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes mellitus by reducing CD36 expression on plasma membranes and intracellular trafficking of glucose transporter type 4 in adipocytes.
source: Recently, VIM deficiency was shown to prevent obesity and insulin resistance in type 2 DM by reducing CD36 expression on plasma membranes and intracellular trafficking of glucose transporter type 4 in adipocytes (Luo et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2021.

claim: This study marks the first demonstration of LBH's efficacy in restoring erectile function in mice with diabetes-induced erectile dysfunction.
source: As far as our knowledge extends, this study marks the first demonstration of LBH's efficacy in restoring erectile function in mice with diabetes-induced ED.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Diabetes was induced by low doses of streptozotocin (50 mg/kg, i.p.) injected for 5 consecutive days.
source: DM was induced as described previously (Jin et al., 2009). Shortly, low doses of streptozotocin (STZ, 50 mg/kg, i.p., Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was injected for 5 consecutive days.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2009.

claim: Only mice with a tail vein blood glucose level higher than 300 mg/dL and significantly decreased body weights were considered to have diabetes mellitus.
source: Eight weeks later, only mice with a tail vein blood glucose level higher than 300 mg/dL and significantly decreased body weights were considered to have DM.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Body weights of streptozotocin-treated (diabetic) mice were significantly lower than those of age-matched non-diabetic controls.
source: Body weights of STZ-treated (diabetic) mice were significantly lower than those of age-matched non-diabetic controls.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Fasting and postprandial blood glucose concentrations were significantly higher in diabetic mice than in non-diabetic controls.
source: Fasting and postprandial blood glucose concentrations were significantly higher in diabetic mice than in non-diabetic controls.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Mean systolic blood pressure was similar in three streptozotocin-treated groups and the non-diabetic control group.
source: MSBP were similar in three STZ-treated groups and the non-diabetic control group (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Supplementary file 2.

claim: Lbh expression in the bladder, heart and aorta, kidney, and trachea was not as specific to pericytes as in penile pericytes.
source: Lbh was expressed in pericytes of the bladder, heart and aorta, kidney, and trachea but not as specifically in penile pericytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: In certain tissues, particularly in mouse penile tissues, Lbh may be a valuable marker in conjunction with other established pericyte marker genes for distinguishing pericytes.
source: Therefore, in certain tissues, particularly in mouse penile tissues, Lbh may be a valuable marker in conjunction with other established pericyte marker genes for distinguishing pericytes.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: LBH is a highly conserved transcription cofactor known to participate in early limb and heart development.
source: Lbh, a highly conserved transcription cofactor, is known to participate in early limb and heart development (Briegel and Joyner, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Briegel and Joyner, 2001.

claim: LBH can directly target the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Moreover, LBH can directly target the Wnt signaling pathway (Rieger et al., 2010) and regulate neural crest cell development (Powder et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rieger et al., 2010.

claim: LBH regulates neural crest cell development.
source: Moreover, LBH can directly target the Wnt signaling pathway (Rieger et al., 2010) and regulate neural crest cell development (Powder et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Powder et al., 2014.

claim: LBH overexpression promotes angiogenesis via VEGF-mediated ERK signaling.
source: In addition, Jiang et al., 2019 showed that LBH overexpression promotes angiogenesis via VEGF-mediated ERK signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claim: LBH inhibits cell migration and angiogenesis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
source: In contrast, LBH inhibits cell migration and angiogenesis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (wu et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to wu et al., 2022 and Wu et al., 2021.

claim: The combination of LBH with CRYAB and VIM could improve neurovascular regeneration in diabetic erectile dysfunction by activating the angiogenic effects of CRYAB and potentially reducing the inflammatory effects of VIM.
source: Therefore, the combination of LBH with CRYAB and VIM could improve neurovascular regeneration in diabetic ED by activating the angiogenic effects of CRYAB and potentially reducing the inflammatory effects of VIM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of LBH, CRYAB, and VIM interactions and their known functions.
